title: Performance triage: 60 seconds and the USE method
part: Part 1 · The box, the way the gurus run it
brief: Ten commands in sixty seconds, then Utilization, Saturation and Errors for every resource. Then check whatever a model tells you about the output.
gurus: Brendan Gregg, Linux Performance Analysis in 60,000 Milliseconds
Brendan Gregg, the USE Method and Systems Performance

exercises.prompt: Match each observation to what it tells you in USE terms.
pairs: vmstat 1: the r column stays above the number of CPUs
mpstat -P ALL 1: one CPU at 100% while the others idle
iostat -xz 1: aqu-sz and r_await climbing on one disk
sar -n DEV 1: rxkB/s near the NIC's line rate
exercises.explain: For every resource: Utilization, Saturation, Errors. The 60-second checklist collects most of these in one pass; PSI adds a direct saturation signal that older checklists did not have.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are in Brendan Gregg's 60-second checklist?
exercises.explain: Ten commands, in that order, from the 2015 Netflix post. The others are fine tools; they are just not the first minute.

exercises.prompt: Finish triage.sh, your 60-second checklist as a script: add per-CPU balance, per-process CPU, disk I/O, memory, network throughput, TCP errors and a top snapshot, and give every interval command a count so the script ends.
exercises.hint: run mpstat -P ALL 1 3, run pidstat 1 3, run iostat -xz 1 3, run free -m, run sar -n DEV 1 3, run sar -n TCP,ETCP 1 3, run top -b -n 1, and change vmstat 1 to vmstat 1 5. mpstat, pidstat, iostat and sar come from the sysstat package.
exercises.explain: This file is the chapter's deliverable: run it first, read it second, and keep the output with the incident. shellcheck keeps it from breaking on the one box where it matters.

checks.name: still opens with uptime, dmesg and vmstat with a count
a top snapshot in batch mode
every interval command has a count, so the script ends

exercises.prompt: Load average is 32 on a 16-CPU box, but mpstat shows the CPUs 70% idle. What is going on?
options: Linux load counts tasks in uninterruptible sleep (usually waiting on disk or NFS) as well as runnable ones; look at I/O
exercises.explain: Linux load averages include D-state tasks, so they measure demand on CPU and disk together. Gregg traced this to a 1993 kernel change in 'Linux Load Averages: Solving the Mystery' (2017). Check iostat -xz 1, vmstat's b column and /proc/pressure/io.

exercises.prompt: The kernel OOM killer fires while you load a large model. Which process does it pick?
options: The one with the highest oom_score, which mostly reflects how much memory it uses, adjusted by oom_score_adj
exercises.explain: /proc/<pid>/oom_score reflects memory use, shifted by oom_score_adj (-1000 to 1000). OOMScoreAdjust= in a unit protects sshd or volunteers a batch job. With cgroup v2, a unit's MemoryMax triggers the kill inside that unit before the whole box runs out.

exercises.prompt: Which bcc / bpftrace tool prints every new process as it is executed, with its arguments?
exercises.answer_text: sudo execsnoop-bpfcc (bcc's execsnoop, as Ubuntu names it)
exercises.explain: Short-lived processes never show up in top. execsnoop catches cron storms, crash-looping helpers, and the script an agent keeps re-running.

exercises.prompt: You paste triage output into a local model. It says the disk is the bottleneck because iostat shows %util 100 on nvme0n1. What do you check before believing it?
options: Whether the device is really saturated: on NVMe and RAID, %util only means busy at some point in each interval, so look at await, aqu-sz and throughput against the device's limits
exercises.explain: The iostat man page warns that %util does not reflect the limits of devices that serve requests in parallel, such as SSDs and RAID arrays. Models repeat the common misreading; verify the claim with the metric that measures saturation.
